title: LabelBench · Different jobs
question: What does the proxy do in LabelBench’s efficient path?
choices: Select examples for oracle annotation.
Replace the oracle’s true labels.
Become the only final evaluated predictor.
Update the pretrained encoder every round.
explanation: The cheap proxy guides acquisition; the final model is fine-tuned end-to-end on the collected labels and remaining unlabeled inputs.

title: LabelBench · Frozen representation
question: Why can cached embeddings be reused during proxy training?
choices: They contain all future oracle labels.
The encoder weights remain fixed on this path.
The proxy never changes.
They are outputs of the final changing encoder.
explanation: The fixed encoder gives a reusable feature representation. Final encoder fine-tuning cannot treat old cached features as current encoder outputs.

title: LabelBench · Acquisition arithmetic
question: For probabilities (0.45, 0.40, 0.15), what is the margin score?
explanation: The margin is the largest probability minus the second largest: 0.45 − 0.40 = 0.05. Margin sampling queries small gaps.

title: LabelBench · Truth versus guesses
question: The selected example was predicted as class 1; the oracle returns class 2. What enters L?
choices: The class 1 pseudo-label.
Both classes with equal confidence.
No label until they agree.
The oracle’s class 2 label.
explanation: Acquisition happens before the hidden target is revealed. The oracle label supplies supervision and can contradict the proxy.

title: LabelBench · Two accuracy tasks
question: With 20 perfect oracle labels in a 100-item pool and 75% accuracy on the other 80, what is pool accuracy?
explanation: The completed pool has 20 correct oracle labels plus 60 correct model labels: 80/100. This is not held-out test accuracy.

title: LabelBench · State in the loop
question: What does the paper specify for proxy training at each acquisition round?
choices: Warm-start the same head forever.
Train the proxy from scratch on the updated partitions.
Retrain the oracle.
Delete previously annotated labels.
explanation: Section 4.1 trains the proxy from scratch. Collected annotations, partitions and cached features survive; proxy weights are not the stated carried state.

title: LabelBench · Uncertainty is not coverage
question: Why might uncertainty sampling select redundant examples?
choices: Uncertainty directly measures pairwise diversity.
Every uncertain image belongs to a rare class.
Duplicates can have the same high uncertainty score.
It reads the hidden labels before ranking.
explanation: High uncertainty alone does not ensure distinct information. Diversity strategies use features or other geometry, with their own representation-dependent limitations.

title: LabelBench · Evidence boundaries
question: What does use of the WILDS datasets establish in this paper?
choices: Distribution-shift robustness is guaranteed.
No pretrained data were used.
The oracle cost includes real annotation time.
The reported evaluation uses in-domain test data.
explanation: The paper uses in-domain splits of iWildCam and fMoW and proposes distribution-shift evaluation as future work. Dataset provenance alone does not establish an OOD result.

title: CEC · Correction
question: What does CEC use to estimate Q(i)?
choices: The top-N predicted class-i probabilities in the unlabeled pool.
Oracle class frequencies for the whole pool.
The held-out test labels.
One shared temperature fitted for every image.
explanation: Q(i) averages the N highest P_i values separately for each class; it uses no oracle targets and need not sum to one.

title: CEC · Entropy
question: With P=(.8,.2) and Q=(.8,.4), what is the calibrated distribution?
explanation: Divide P by Q to get (1,.5), then normalize by 1.5. The intermediate scores are not a probability distribution.

title: CEC · Neighbor
question: Which expression matches the neighbor uncertainty in paper Eq. 6?
choices: Divide the weighted entropy sum by the sum of distance weights.
Divide the distance-weighted neighbor entropy sum by k.
Multiply all neighbor entropies by self-entropy.
Return zero whenever a neighbor is confident.
explanation: The denominator is k, the number of neighbors. Distance attenuation reduces the contribution rather than being normalized away.

title: CEC · Additive
question: If an image has high self-entropy and confident neighbors, does CEC automatically reject it?
choices: Yes, because U is a product.
Yes, because it applies a hard AND test.
Yes, because neighbors replace the self term.
No: U adds the self and neighbor terms.
explanation: Eq. 7 is additive. Neighbor uncertainty supplies a preference for shared confusion, not a hard outlier veto.

title: CEC · Center
question: After uncertainty-weighted K-means, which image does CEC query in each cluster?
choices: The real image closest to the weighted center.
The image with the largest uncertainty regardless of its position.
A generated synthetic image at the center.
An image chosen using the hidden true class.
explanation: CEC weights clustering first, then queries center-nearest real images. Greedy highest-entropy selection after ordinary clustering is a different rule.

title: CEC · Gradient
question: In the main CoOp setting, what does labeled cross-entropy update?
choices: All image and text encoder weights.
The oracle label distribution.
The learnable context vectors, through the frozen text encoder.
Only the acquisition cluster centers.
explanation: Frozen text-encoder weights still permit gradients with respect to context inputs. Learned context changes text features and future class probabilities.

title: CEC · State
question: What carries forward into the next prompt-training round under the source settings?
choices: Only the most recent batch of pseudo-labels.
All collected oracle labels; CLIP is reloaded and prompts trained on accumulated data.
The unlabeled pool with queried images still included.
A guaranteed equal number of labels per class.
explanation: The paper describes reloading zero-shot CLIP each round and training on accumulated D_L. Queried images leave D_U; class balance is not guaranteed.

title: CEC · Evidence
question: Textures at 2%: CEC accuracy is 52.8%, random is 44.2%. What does this support?
choices: CEC always beats zero-shot CLIP on every dataset.
CEC improves accuracy by 8.6% relative to random.
CEC is 52.8% faster at acquisition.
CEC gains 8.6 percentage points in this reported test setting.
explanation: Subtract the reported accuracies: 52.8−44.2=8.6 points. These are held-out CoOp/ViT-B/16 results across three seeds, not a universal guarantee or runtime measurement.

title: Active Prompt · Soft representation
question: What weights each class text feature in Active Prompt’s mixture?
choices: The true pool label.
The model’s predicted class probability.
The cluster’s population only.
The class-specific annotation price.
explanation: Eq. (6) uses soft predicted probabilities, preserving competing-class evidence before any oracle query.

title: Active Prompt · Feature blocks
question: If image and weighted-text features each have dimension d, what does concatenation produce?
choices: A d-dimensional sum.
A class-label integer.
A 2d-dimensional feature.
A vector with exactly C entries.
explanation: Eq. (7) retains separate image and text-mixture blocks, each of dimension d. The probability vector has C entries.

title: Active Prompt · Cluster balance
question: When B equals the number of classes, does selecting one image per cluster guarantee one true label per class?
choices: Yes, because K-means knows the labels.
Yes, because every cluster is a class.
Only when confidence exceeds 0.5.
No; feature clusters can cross class boundaries.
explanation: The method uses unlabeled features and predictions. Cluster-balanced coverage is not perfect true-class balance.

title: Active Prompt · Class-specific gate
question: A candidate predicts A at 0.80. Thresholds are ε_A=0.85 and ε_B=0.60. What happens?
choices: Query a human label.
Accept pseudo-label A because 0.80 exceeds ε_B.
Accept pseudo-label B.
Discard the example from the candidate set.
explanation: The gate compares with the predicted class’s threshold. Since 0.80 < 0.85, the oracle supplies a target.

title: Active Prompt · Boundary decision
question: What does Eq. (12) prescribe when candidate confidence equals its predicted class threshold?
choices: Query the oracle.
Accept the pseudo-label.
Remove all previous pseudo-labels.
Reset the frozen encoders.
explanation: The pseudo branch uses ≥; the human-query branch uses <. Passing the gate does not prove correctness.

title: Active Prompt · Persistent state
question: What is carried forward when prompts are randomly reinitialized each round?
choices: Only the previous prompt parameters.
Newly revealed test labels.
The accumulated dataset, including earlier assigned pseudo targets.
A freshly trained image encoder.
explanation: Eq. (12) retains D_(r−1), and Eq. (13) trains a reset prompt on all D_r. The encoders remain frozen.

title: Active Prompt · Annotation arithmetic
question: Two rounds select two images each; round one queries both, round two queries one and pseudo-labels one. What are the totals?
choices: Four training targets and four human queries.
Three training targets and four human queries.
Two training targets and three human queries.
Four training targets and three human queries.
explanation: A pseudo-label grows the training set without a human annotation: four targets, three purchases. The 25% toy saving is not the paper’s reported 17.6%.

title: Active Prompt · Evidence scope
question: Why is Table 1’s CB* not ordinary hidden-label acquisition?
choices: It uses true-label text features to construct the dataset.
It uses frozen image features.
It performs K-means clustering.
It trains small prompts rather than all weights.
explanation: CB* replaces soft predicted text mixtures with ground-truth class text. It is an oracle-assisted comparison with label-balanced few-shot datasets.
